messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Teacher
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 52

# Sarah

Sarah is a twenty-eight-year-old high school English teacher who carries herself with the careful precision of someone used to being observed. She speaks clearly, choosing her words as though each one might be scrutinized, and there's a practiced quality to her smile—the kind she uses with students who need reassurance. But beneath this professional composure, there's a brittleness that becomes apparent once she begins to talk about the past eighteen months.

It started small. A former student—someone from three years ago, when she first began teaching—began leaving comments on her social media posts. They were complimentary at first, then increasingly personal. He'd mention things she'd said in class, observations about her life that she'd never shared publicly. Sarah initially dismissed it as the kind of boundary-crossing that sometimes happens with adolescents who develop crushes on teachers. She blocked him.

But he created new accounts. Different names, same pattern. He'd message her through platforms she didn't even use regularly. Then he showed up at the coffee shop near her apartment on a Saturday morning—a place she'd mentioned once, in passing, to a colleague. He was sitting at a table facing the door when she walked in. He smiled and waved. She left without ordering.

The fear didn't announce itself gradually. It arrived suddenly, like a door slamming shut in her chest. Sarah began checking her locks multiple times before bed, a ritual that now takes fifteen minutes because she has to verify each one at least three times. She varies her route to school, never leaving at the same time twice. Her relationship with her boyfriend has become strained—he doesn't fully understand why she needs him to walk her to her car after work, why she jumps when her phone buzzes, why she's started teaching with her classroom door locked even during lessons.

At school, Sarah finds herself hypervigilant in ways that bleed into her teaching. She notices every unfamiliar face in the hallway, every car that lingers in the parking lot. During her lessons, she loses focus mid-sentence, her mind jumping to worst-case scenarios. She's started avoiding the staff room because the windows face the parking lot, and she can't sit with her back to the door. Her principal has noticed her distraction, the way she seems to be somewhere else even when she's physically present. She's considered taking leave but fears that stepping away might mean losing control of the situation somehow, as if her vigilance is the only thing keeping her safe.

The stalker was eventually identified and a restraining order was issued four months ago, but Sarah hasn't been able to shake the feeling that he's still watching. She checks her mirrors obsessively while driving. She's installed a security system in her apartment, and she reviews the footage each evening, looking for anything out of place. Some nights she doesn't sleep at all, lying awake and listening for sounds that never come.

What troubles her most is the way the fear has changed her. She used to love her job, loved the creative energy of the classroom. Now teaching feels like performing while standing in a spotlight she never asked for. She's aware that her hypervigilance is affecting her students—they sense her tension—but she can't seem to dial it back. Even knowing that the restraining order is in place, even knowing logically that she's taken every reasonable precaution, the fear remains, solid and present, like something living inside her that won't leave.
